R.q:
Dr. Lena Park, the economist who testified in favor of the proposed soda tax, presented data from two cities where soda purchases fell by about 20 percent after similar taxes took effect. But what would she know about the lives of working families? Dr. Park lives in a wealthy suburb, drives a luxury car and has probably never had to stretch a grocery budget. The council should reject this tax.

How does the author mainly attempt to discredit the case for the soda tax?
o: By questioning whether the two cities Dr. Park studied resemble this one
By attacking Dr. Park's personal life instead of responding to her data
By presenting data from other cities that contradict Dr. Park's findings
By explaining how the tax would raise grocery costs for working families
R.w: The author never addresses the 20 percent drop. Instead, the author points to where Dr. Park lives and what she drives. Attacking the person rather than the evidence (an ad hominem attack) is a sign of bias.

n.0: Questioning whether the cities are comparable would be a fair challenge to her evidence, but the author never raises it.
n.2: The author offers no data of any kind; the only figures in the passage are Dr. Park's.
n.3: The author mentions working families but never explains any effect of the tax on grocery costs; the focus stays on Dr. Park herself.

R.q:
Read the passage.

When the city of Linden widened Route 9 from two lanes to four, planners expected rush-hour jams to disappear. Within three years, however, delays were nearly as long as before. Traffic counts showed that many more cars now used the road. Surveys found that some drivers had switched to Route 9 from other roads, others now drove at rush hour instead of earlier or later, and some families had moved to new subdivisions built along the wider road. Researchers call this pattern induced demand: adding road space can attract enough new traffic to fill it.

Which statement accurately reflects the cause-and-effect relationship described in the passage?
o: Drivers avoided Route 9 after the widening because construction made it slower.
Longer rush-hour delays caused families to move away from the Route 9 corridor.
Widening Route 9 attracted more drivers, which brought rush-hour delays back.
New subdivisions along Route 9 brought more drivers, so the city widened it.
R.w: The order in the passage is: the road was widened, more drivers began using it (switching roads, changing times, moving nearby), and delays returned. The widening is the cause and the added traffic and delays are the effects.

n.0: Contradicted: traffic counts show many more cars used Route 9 after the widening.
n.1: Opposite: families moved to new subdivisions along the road, not away from it.
n.3: Reverses cause and effect: the subdivisions were built along the wider road, after the widening.

R.q: Read the passage. Select the word or phrase that signals that one event caused another.

parts: The town of Millbrook has added fluoride to its water

parts.t: since
During

parts: the same period, the number of cavities found in school dental screenings fell by nearly half.

parts.t: By contrast

parts: , a nearby town without fluoride saw only a small drop.

parts.t: Because of

parts: these results, the county health board voted to expand the program to three more towns.

parts.t: Meanwhile

parts: , some residents continue to question the cost.

R.w: "Because of" links the screening results to the board's vote: the results are the cause and the vote is the effect.

n.a: Here "since" marks a starting point in time (since 1998). It can signal cause in other sentences, but not in this one.
n.b: "During" places the drop in cavities within a time period. It does not state that one event produced another.
n.c: "By contrast" signals a difference between the two towns, not a cause.
n.e: "Meanwhile" signals that two things are happening at the same time. It introduces an ongoing objection, not an effect.

R.q:
Several nurses on 4 West have proposed moving the morning shift change from 7:00 to 6:30 a.m. so that handoff reports finish before the 7:00 medications are due. They point out that nurses now give morning medications late on most days. The unit manager rejected the idea: "Shift change has been at 7:00 since this hospital opened in 1974. It has worked for fifty years, and I see no reason to change it now."

Which fallacy does the manager's response contain?
o: Hasty generalization
False dilemma
Bandwagon
Appeal to tradition
R.w: The manager defends the 7:00 shift change because it has been done that way since 1974, without answering the nurses' point about late medications. Arguing that something is right because it is long-standing is an appeal to tradition.

n.0: The manager does not generalize from a few examples.
n.1: The manager does not reduce the issue to two options.
n.2: Bandwagon appeals to what many people currently do or believe; the manager appeals to history.

R.q:
In a report on a hospital's new staffing model, the author writes: "Letting nurses design their own schedules through a shared online calendar is a bold experiment, and early results are encouraging. Overtime fell by 18 percent in the first quarter, and fewer nurses left the unit."

By calling the staffing model "a bold experiment," the author suggests that the model is
o: a daring new approach that deserves credit.
a careless gamble with nurses' schedules.
a proven method that other units already use.
a costly plan that the hospital should reconsider.
R.w: "Bold" carries a positive connotation of admirable daring, and "experiment" marks the model as new and untested. Together with "early results are encouraging," the word choice presents the model as a risk worth praising.

n.1: "Careless gamble" gives risk-taking a negative connotation. The author calls the results "encouraging," so the attitude is approving, not critical.
n.2: "Experiment" and "early results" show the model is new and still being tested, so it is not presented as proven or borrowed from other units.
n.3: The passage reports falling overtime and fewer nurses leaving and raises no cost concern, so nothing suggests the hospital should reconsider.

R.q:
Vitamin D is unusual among vitamins because the body can make it. When skin is exposed to the ultraviolet B (UVB) rays in sunlight, it produces a form of vitamin D that the liver and kidneys then activate. The amount of UVB reaching the ground depends on the angle of the sun. In winter, at places north of about 37 degrees latitude, the sun sits so low that little UVB reaches the ground, and the skin makes little vitamin D however long a person stays outside. Foods such as fatty fish, eggs, and fortified milk also supply the vitamin. Harborview lies at 42 degrees north latitude; Palmetto lies at 33 degrees north.

Based on the passage, which conclusion is best supported?
o: Residents of Harborview can make up for winter by spending more hours outdoors.
Winter sunlight gives Harborview residents less vitamin D than it gives Palmetto residents.
Residents of Harborview have lower vitamin D levels all year than residents of Palmetto.
Residents of Palmetto do not need vitamin D from food during the winter months.
R.w: Two details combine: north of about 37 degrees, winter sun produces little vitamin D in skin, and Harborview (42 degrees) is north of that line while Palmetto (33 degrees) is south of it.

n.0: This contradicts the passage: north of 37 degrees in winter, the skin makes little vitamin D however long a person stays outside.
n.2: The passage limits the latitude effect to winter and says food also supplies vitamin D, so year-round levels cannot be concluded.
n.3: The passage says Palmetto residents can make vitamin D from winter sun, but it does not say they need none from food.

R.q:
The Lot on Fifth Street
They paved the field where I used to run,
poured gray over clover, wall over sun.
But one old oak they could not move
still splits the sidewalk, groove by groove.
Each spring it pushes, slow and sure,
a crack, a root, a little more,
till weeds and sparrows find the seam
and green comes back like a half-remembered dream.

Which theme does the poem express?
o: Nature can slowly reclaim what people have tried to cover over.
Childhood memories fade as familiar places change over time.
The speaker regrets having moved away from the old field.
Cities should protect their oldest trees from new construction.
R.w: The poem moves from paving over the field to the oak slowly splitting the sidewalk until weeds and birds return. Its message is nature's slow return through what people built.

n.1: The poem's central movement is the oak and weeds breaking back through the pavement; its one image of memory describes the green returning, not the speaker's memories fading.
n.2: The poem never says the speaker moved away; regret about leaving is not in the text.
n.3: This is a policy recommendation; the poem describes and reflects but never argues for protecting trees.

R.q:
You wake at 4:30 a.m., before the alarm, because your body has learned the schedule. You pull on scrubs in the dark so you will not wake anyone, grab the lunch you packed last night and drive through empty streets to the hospital. By 6:45 you are taking report from the night nurse, and by 7:15 you have already answered three call lights. Your feet ache by noon. Still, when a patient squeezes your hand and thanks you, you remember why you chose this work.

From which point of view is the passage written?
o: first person
third person limited
third person objective
second person
R.w: The narration addresses the reader directly as "you" and places the reader in the role of the nurse. That is second-person point of view.

n.0: The passage reads like a personal memory, but no "I" or "we" appears; every action is assigned to "you."
n.1: Third-person limited would describe a character as "he" or "she" and reveal that character's thoughts.
n.2: Third-person objective would describe characters from outside using "he" or "she," reporting only actions and speech.

R.q:
In 2019, the town of Ridgeway closed its only grocery store. As a result, many residents began buying most of their food at gas stations and dollar stores. Because of the distance to the nearest supermarket, 12 miles away, families without cars ate fewer fresh fruits and vegetables. For example, a survey by the county health department found that produce purchases fell by half. Meanwhile, rates of diabetes in the town continued to rise. In contrast, a neighboring town that kept its grocery store saw little change. The store's closing led to a new effort to start a weekly farmers market.

Which phrases from the passage signal a cause-and-effect relationship? Select all that apply.
o: Meanwhile
In contrast
Because of
led to
For example
As a result
R.w: "As a result" introduces an effect of the closing, "Because of" introduces a cause of the change in eating habits, and "led to" links the closing to the farmers market effort. All three signal cause and effect.

n.0: "Meanwhile" signals that two things happened at the same time, a time relationship rather than a causal one.
n.1: "In contrast" signals a difference between two towns, which is a compare-and-contrast signal.
n.4: "For example" introduces supporting evidence (the survey), not a cause or effect.

R.q:
The Marlow River Bridge will close for repairs on June 1 and stay closed for three months. During the closure, drivers will detour across the Oak Street Bridge, two miles north. When the Marlow bridge closed for one weekend last fall, a traffic study found that travel times across the Oak Street Bridge doubled during morning and evening rush hours, while midday traffic was barely affected. The city has asked large employers to consider flexible start times during the repairs.

Which prediction about the summer is best supported by the passage?
o: Midday trips across the Oak Street Bridge will likely take about double their usual time.
Rush-hour trips across the Oak Street Bridge will likely take longer than usual.
The repairs will last longer than three months because of the heavy detour traffic.
Large employers will require their workers to start later until the bridge reopens.
R.w: The weekend study showed Oak Street travel times doubling at rush hour when the Marlow bridge closed. A three-month closure puts the same cause in motion, so longer rush-hour trips are the supported prediction.

n.0: This uses the wrong part of the study: travel times doubled at rush hour, while midday traffic was barely affected.
n.2: The passage gives no reason to expect the repairs to run over; traffic on the detour does not affect the repair schedule.
n.3: The city only asked employers to consider flexible start times; a requirement is not supported.

R.q:
Ethan is researching the 1972 flood that destroyed much of downtown Millbrook. At the county historical society, he finds the following items:
A. A photograph of Main Street taken by a newspaper photographer on the day of the flood
B. An oral history interview, recorded in 2005, with a man who was rescued from his roof in 1972
C. A 2022 newspaper article looking back on the flood's 50th anniversary
D. The Millbrook town council minutes from its emergency meeting in June 1972
E. A local history book, published in 1990, with a chapter analyzing the flood
F. A state encyclopedia entry summarizing major floods in the region

Which items are primary sources? Select all that apply.
o: Item E
Item F
Item C
Item D
Item B
Item A
R.w: The photograph (A) and the council minutes (D) were created during the event. The oral history (B) is an eyewitness account by a survivor, which makes it primary even though it was recorded decades later.

n.0: A history book analyzing the flood interprets primary sources, so it is secondary.
n.1: An encyclopedia entry compiles summaries from other sources, so it is tertiary.
n.2: An anniversary article looks back on and interprets the flood, so it is secondary.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Start with the word PULSE. Carry out the steps below in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Write the word backward.
2. Replace the second letter with the letter that comes two places before it in the alphabet.
3. Repeat the last letter so that it appears twice at the end.
4. Remove every vowel except the first vowel in the word.
5. Insert the letter A after the third letter.

Which of the following is the final result?
o: EQLAP
EQLAPP
ELPAP
EQLPAP
R.w: Step 1: ESLUP. Step 2 replaces S with Q (two places before S): EQLUP. Step 3: EQLUPP. Step 4 keeps the first vowel (E) and removes U: EQLPP. Step 5 inserts A after the third letter (L): EQLAPP.

n.0: Skips step 3, so only one P remains at the end.
n.2: Counts two places after S (U) instead of before it; step 4 then removes that U too.
n.3: Off by one: A was inserted after the fourth letter instead of the third.

R.q:
A school nurse is choosing an online article about managing asthma during exercise to send to the families of students on the track team. She has narrowed her search to one article that seems clear and useful, but the page gives few details about where the information came from. Before she shares it, she wants to know whether the article can be trusted.

Which detail would most increase the article's credibility?
o: It was written by a parent whose two children both have asthma.
It has been shared thousands of times on social media this year.
It includes colorful infographics that explain the steps clearly.
It was written by a lung specialist and cites peer-reviewed studies.
R.w: A qualified author (authority) and citations to peer-reviewed research (accuracy) are core credibility markers.

n.0: A parent's experience is personal and anecdotal; it lacks medical authority.
n.1: Popularity measures reach, not accuracy; misinformation is often widely shared.
n.2: Clear design helps readability but says nothing about whether the content is correct.

R.q:
Marisol, a nursing student, is preparing a teaching sheet for a patient who has just been prescribed a new blood thinner. She wants to list the foods and other medicines that can interact with it. Her options are the official prescribing information published with the drug, a health news website's article about the drug's approval, a popular health app's summary written by its staff, and a pharmacology textbook printed before the drug was approved.

Which source is best for this purpose?
o: The official prescribing information for the drug
The pharmacology textbook printed before approval
The health news article about the drug's approval
The health app's summary written by its staff
R.w: The official prescribing information lists the drug's known interactions in detail and is the authoritative, product-specific source.

n.1: A textbook printed before the drug was approved cannot include it.
n.2: A news article about approval gives a general story, not a complete list of interactions.
n.3: An app's staff summary is secondhand and may leave out details.

R.q:
The new QuickCare urgent care center on Route 9 is the best thing to happen to Fairview in years. Wait times average 15 minutes, the staff is friendly, and the building is spotless. The center accepts most major insurance plans and is open seven days a week from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Families who have been driving 40 minutes to the county hospital for minor injuries finally have a better option close to home.

Which additional fact about the writer of this review would most strongly suggest that the review is biased?
o: The writer visited the center twice before writing the review.
The writer has written health columns for the paper for six years.
The writer lives about 2 miles from the new center.
The writer is a part owner of the QuickCare center.
R.w: A part owner profits when the center attracts patients. That financial interest gives the writer a reason to present the center favorably, which is an undisclosed interest and a strong sign of bias.

n.0: Visiting the center more than once is firsthand experience; it does not give the writer a stake in the outcome.
n.1: Years of experience writing health columns adds credibility and creates no conflict of interest.
n.2: Living nearby may explain the writer's interest in the center, but it gives no personal gain from praising it.

R.q: Read the passage. Select the sentence that describes the earliest event in the story.

parts.t: By the time the ambulance reached Mercy Hospital, Tomas had already called his sister.
He had found his grandfather on the kitchen floor that afternoon, a few minutes after returning from the hardware store.
Earlier that day, his grandfather had complained of feeling dizzy but had insisted that Tomas run the errand anyway.
Before calling his sister, Tomas had dialed 911 and followed the dispatcher's instructions to keep his grandfather still.
Now, sitting in the waiting room, Tomas wished he had stayed home.

sn.a: By the time the ambulance reached Mercy Hospital, Tomas had already called his sister.
sn.b: He had found his grandfather on the kitchen floor that afternoon, a few minutes after returning from the hardware store.
sn.c: Earlier that day, his grandfather had complained of feeling dizzy but had insisted that Tomas run the errand anyway.
sn.d: Before calling his sister, Tomas had dialed 911 and followed the dispatcher's instructions to keep his grandfather still.
sn.e: Now, sitting in the waiting room, Tomas wished he had stayed home.

R.w: In time order: the grandfather complains of dizziness and sends Tomas on the errand (sentence 3); Tomas returns and finds him (sentence 2); he calls 911 (sentence 4); he calls his sister (sentence 1); and he waits at the hospital (sentence 5). "Earlier that day" and the fact that the complaint came before the errand place sentence 3 first.

n.a: This is mentioned first, but the ambulance's arrival comes near the end of the events. Order of mention is not order of occurrence.
n.b: Finding his grandfather happened after Tomas returned from the errand, and the errand came after the dizziness complaint.
n.d: The 911 call came after Tomas found his grandfather, which was after the complaint earlier that day.
n.e: The waiting room is the story's present moment, the latest event described.

R.q:
For a child development class, Tyler wrote a report arguing that parents should limit preschoolers' screen time to two hours a day. His only source is a 1999 pamphlet from a parenting group, printed before most families owned smartphones or tablets. The pamphlet discusses television viewing and recommends the two-hour limit. Tyler did not check whether the group or any health agency has updated its advice since then.

What is the main weakness of the evidence Tyler uses?
o: It is unrelated to the subject of screen time for preschool children.
It comes from a source with a financial interest in the advice it gives.
It is too dated for a topic on which guidance may have since changed.
It is a personal story about one child rather than general guidance.
R.w: The pamphlet is from 1999, before smartphones and tablets were common, and Tyler never checked for updated advice. For a fast-changing topic, an old source lacks currency.

n.0: The pamphlet addresses children's screen viewing, so it is related to the topic.
n.1: The passage gives no sign that the parenting group profits from its advice.
n.3: The pamphlet offers a general recommendation, not one child's story.

R.q:
Two years ago, Cedar Ridge Hospital began letting its nurses choose either 8-hour or 12-hour shifts. In a recent staff survey, 70 percent of nurses on 12-hour shifts said they had more days available for family, compared with 35 percent of nurses on 8-hour shifts. However, 40 percent of nurses on 12-hour shifts said they felt very tired at the end of a shift, compared with 25 percent of those on 8-hour shifts. The rate at which nurses left the hospital was similar in both groups.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Most nurses at Cedar Ridge Hospital now prefer 12-hour shifts to 8-hour shifts.
Nurses on 8-hour shifts are less likely than others to leave the hospital.
Nurses on 12-hour shifts tend to trade more fatigue for more days with family.
Twelve-hour shifts lead to more patient care errors than 8-hour shifts.
R.w: Nurses on 12-hour shifts were twice as likely to report more family days (70% vs 35%) and also more likely to feel very tired (40% vs 25%), so the passage supports a trade-off.

n.0: The passage gives survey results within each group but not how many nurses chose each shift, so preference cannot be concluded.
n.1: This contradicts the passage, which says the rate of leaving was similar in both groups.
n.3: Patient errors are never mentioned; this relies on outside assumptions rather than the text.

R.q:
For a paper on nursing during the American Civil War, Andre is using two sources.
Source A: the diary kept by a volunteer nurse at a Union hospital in Washington, D.C., from 1862 to 1864
Source B: a 2015 book by a historian who compares the diaries of 30 Civil War nurses and explains what they reveal about hospital conditions
His bibliography must label each source correctly.

Which statement correctly classifies both sources?
o: Source A is secondary, and Source B is primary.
Both are primary, since Source B quotes diaries.
Source A is primary, and Source B is secondary.
Source A is primary, and Source B is tertiary.
R.w: Step 1: the diary is a firsthand account written at the time, so Source A is primary. Step 2: the historian's book analyzes and interprets those diaries, so Source B is secondary.

n.0: This reverses the categories: the diary is the firsthand record, and the book interprets it.
n.1: Quoting primary sources does not make a book primary; its author interprets others' accounts.
n.3: Source B offers original analysis; tertiary sources such as encyclopedias only compile summaries.

R.q:
From a website that reviews nutrition books: "The Greenleaf Diet Guide is the most reliable guide on the market. We know it can be trusted because it is the most dependable source of diet advice available today. Readers who want accurate information should choose it over every other guide." The review does not name the guide's author, describe the author's training, or list any of the sources the guide uses.

Which statement best describes the flaw in the review's reasoning?
o: It attacks the authors of other guides instead of judging their advice.
It gives a reason for trusting the guide that restates its own claim.
It trusts the guide because a well-known person has recommended it.
It judges the guide by the number of readers who have bought a copy.
R.w: "Most reliable" is supported only by "most dependable," which says the same thing in other words. The conclusion is used as its own premise, which is circular reasoning.

n.0: Other guides are mentioned only in passing; their authors are not attacked.
n.2: No person is named as recommending the guide, so this is not an appeal to authority.
n.3: The review never mentions sales or popularity.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Directions for Use
Take one tablet by mouth every 12 hours, with food. Swallow the tablet whole; do not crush or chew it. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if your next dose is due in less than 4 hours, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose. Store at room temperature, away from moisture.

Jordan takes his doses at 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. At 5 p.m., he realizes that he forgot his 8 a.m. dose.

According to the directions, what should Jordan do?
o: Take the missed dose now with food, then take his next dose at 8 p.m.
Take two tablets with food at 8 p.m. to make up for the missed dose.
Skip the missed dose and take his next dose at 8 p.m. as usual.
Take the missed dose now and move his next dose to 5 a.m. tomorrow.
R.w: At 5 p.m., Jordan's next dose (8 p.m.) is due in 3 hours, which is less than 4. The "However" exception applies: skip the missed dose and take the next one at the usual time.

n.0: Follows the general rule but misses the exception: with the next dose only 3 hours away, the missed dose is skipped.
n.1: The directions forbid taking two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
n.3: The directions never say to shift the schedule; with the next dose under 4 hours away, the missed dose is skipped.

R.q:
When Rosa Jimenez, 58, felt a sudden ache in her jaw while gardening, she assumed she had pulled a muscle. Two hours later, she was in a cardiac unit. Rosa's experience is common. Women having a heart attack often notice symptoms other than chest pain, such as jaw or back pain, nausea, shortness of breath or unusual fatigue. Because these symptoms are less familiar, women often wait longer than men before seeking care. Doctors advise anyone with these symptoms to call 911 rather than drive to the hospital.

Why does the author most likely begin the passage with Rosa Jimenez's experience?
o: to show that jaw pain is the most common symptom in women
to entertain readers with a dramatic story
to draw readers in with a real example of the problem
to argue that gardening is risky for older adults
R.w: The anecdote puts a human face on the problem the passage goes on to explain: women's heart attack symptoms are often missed. An opening story in an informational text usually serves to engage the reader and introduce the topic.

n.0: Jaw pain is listed as one of several possible symptoms; the passage does not rank it as the most common.
n.1: The story is dramatic, but it introduces factual health information; the passage as a whole informs rather than entertains.
n.3: Gardening is simply what Rosa was doing; the passage never suggests that gardening caused her heart attack.

R.q:
Read the price table.

Riverbend Fitness Membership Options
Plan | Monthly fee | Joining fee | Includes
Basic | $25 | $50 | Gym floor, 5 a.m. to 9 p.m.
Plus | $40 | $50 | Gym floor 24 hours, group classes
Family (up to 4 people) | $70 | none | Plus benefits for each member
Student (with school ID) | $20 | none | Basic benefits
Members age 65 and older pay 20 percent less than the listed monthly fee for any plan. Joining fees are not discounted.

Carmen is 67 years old. She wants a membership for herself that includes group classes. Based on the table, what will her monthly fee be?
R.w: Group classes come with the Plus plan ($40 a month). Carmen is over 65, so she pays 20 percent less: $40 - $8 = $32.

n.0: $40 is the Plus fee before the senior discount.
n.1: $56 is the discounted Family plan, which is for up to four people; Carmen needs a membership for herself.
n.2: $20 is the Basic plan with the senior discount ($25 - $5), and Basic does not include group classes.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Bayview Community College: Associate Degree in Nursing
Program Length: The program takes four semesters to complete after prerequisites. Most students finish in two years, attending full time.
Clinical Experience: Students complete 180 hours of supervised clinical practice in the first year and 240 hours in the second year, for a total of 420 hours. First-year clinicals take place at Bayview General Hospital; second-year students may also rotate through the county health department and two long-term care centers.
Skills Lab: In addition, each semester includes 45 hours in the on-campus simulation lab, where students practice procedures on mannequins before performing them with patients.

According to the passage, how many hours of supervised clinical practice does a student complete in the second year?
o: 240 hours
420 hours
330 hours
180 hours
R.w: The Clinical Experience section states 240 hours of supervised clinical practice in the second year.

n.1: 420 hours is the total for both years.
n.2: Adds the second year's two semesters of simulation lab (90 hours), which the passage lists separately from clinical practice.
n.3: 180 hours is the first-year figure.

R.q:
Read the timeline.

Measles in the United States: Selected Events
1912: Measles becomes a nationally reportable disease.
1954: The measles virus is first isolated in a laboratory.
1963: The first measles vaccine is licensed.
1968: An improved measles vaccine is licensed.
1971: The combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is licensed.
1989: A second dose of measles vaccine is recommended for children.
2000: Measles is declared eliminated from the United States.

According to the timeline, how many years passed between the licensing of the first measles vaccine and the declaration that measles had been eliminated from the United States?
o: 37 years
46 years
11 years
29 years
R.w: The first vaccine was licensed in 1963 and elimination was declared in 2000: 2000 - 1963 = 37 years.

n.1: Counts from 1954, when the virus was isolated, not when a vaccine was licensed.
n.2: Counts from 1989, when the second dose was recommended.
n.3: Counts from 1971, when the MMR vaccine was licensed, not the first measles vaccine.

R.q:
I still remember Sunday mornings in my grandmother's kitchen: the radio playing gospel music, the smell of biscuits and coffee, and the yellow curtains she sewed herself. My cousins and I would crowd around the table while she told stories about growing up in Georgia. Grandma is ninety now and lives in a bright apartment near my parents, but whenever I smell fresh biscuits, I am eight years old again, waiting for the first one to cool.

Which word best describes the tone of the passage?
o: mournful
indifferent
humorous
nostalgic
R.w: The author recalls a cherished past with warm sensory details and a longing to return to it ("I am eight years old again"). A fond, wistful attitude toward the past is a nostalgic tone.

n.0: "Mournful" suggests grief over a loss. The grandmother is alive and well, and the memories are warm rather than sad.
n.1: "Indifferent" means not caring, but the vivid, affectionate details show the author cares deeply.
n.2: The passage is warm, not joking; no detail is meant to make the reader laugh.

R.q:
Read the passage.

When Lorraine Whitfield finished nursing school in 1971, the nearest hospital to her hometown in rural Mississippi was a ninety-minute drive away. She spent her first years working night shifts in the city and driving home on weekends to check on neighbors who had no doctor. In 1978 she persuaded a church congregation to donate an old school bus, which she and two volunteers fitted with an exam table, a refrigerator for vaccines and a folding ramp. For the next twenty years, the bus visited eleven towns on a fixed weekly route. By the time Whitfield retired, the county had opened two permanent clinics, both built at stops where the bus had drawn the longest lines.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Lorraine Whitfield worked night shifts in a city hospital before moving back to rural Mississippi.
Rural Mississippi counties needed more hospitals in the 1970s than the state's cities did.
Lorraine Whitfield brought regular care to underserved towns, which helped lead to permanent clinics.
A church donated a school bus that volunteers turned into a mobile clinic in 1978.
R.w: The passage follows Whitfield from seeing the lack of nearby care, to building a mobile clinic, to twenty years of weekly visits, to permanent clinics built at the busiest stops. The main idea links her work to that lasting result.

n.0: Distortion and too narrow: she drove home on weekends, and the passage never says she moved back; this is also only an early detail.
n.1: Too broad and outside the passage: it never compares how many hospitals cities and rural counties needed.
n.3: Too narrow: the donated bus is one event in the story, not the point the whole passage makes.

R.q:
Read the notice.

Starting July 1, Clearwater residents will sort recycling into two bins instead of one. The blue bin is for paper and cardboard: newspapers, mail, cereal boxes and flattened shipping boxes. The green bin is for containers: glass bottles and jars, aluminum and steel cans, and plastic bottles and tubs marked with a 1, 2 or 5. Containers should be rinsed, but labels may be left on. Plastic bags, foam cups, foam takeout containers and greasy pizza boxes go in the trash, not in either bin. Pickup will remain every other Thursday.

According to the notice, which item belongs in the green bin?
o: A flattened cereal box from the kitchen pantry
A rinsed plastic tub marked with the number 6
A clean foam coffee cup from a nearby cafe
A rinsed glass salsa jar with its label still on
R.w: Glass jars go in the green bin, containers should be rinsed, and labels may be left on.

n.0: Cereal boxes are paper products and go in the blue bin.
n.1: The green bin takes plastic tubs marked 1, 2 or 5, so a tub marked 6 is not accepted.
n.2: Foam cups go in the trash.

R.q:
For five years, Northline Grocery has followed the same pattern. Each spring it opens a new store in a town where its home delivery service has already grown past 500 customers. This year, delivery customers passed 500 in two towns, Carver and Danbury. Northline has signed a lease on an empty building in Carver that once housed a furniture store. A local news report says Danbury has no available building large enough for a grocery store, and no new construction is planned there.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage?
o: Northline will most likely open new stores in both Carver and Danbury next spring.
Northline will end its delivery service in Carver once the store opens.
Northline will most likely open a new store in Carver next spring.
Northline will open a store in Danbury before it opens one in Carver.
R.w: Carver meets Northline's usual condition (over 500 delivery customers) and the company has already leased a building there, so a spring opening in Carver fits the five-year pattern.

n.0: Danbury meets the customer condition, but it has no suitable building and no planned construction, so a store there next spring is not supported.
n.1: The passage says nothing about ending delivery after a store opens; this needs an unstated event.
n.3: Danbury lacks a building while Carver has a signed lease, so the passage points the other way.

R.q:
As a pharmacist for twenty years, I have watched patients struggle to open childproof medicine caps. Those caps have saved countless children from accidental poisonings, and I would never want them removed from homes with young children. But many of my older customers have arthritis, and some of them leave their bottles open on the counter because they cannot reopen them. Federal rules already allow patients to request easy-open caps. Pharmacies should make that choice clear to every customer over sixty-five who lives without children.

Which of the following best describes the author's point of view on childproof caps?
o: They should be removed from all prescription bottles.
They are useful but should be optional for some patients.
They are a federal requirement that pharmacies cannot change.
They have failed to prevent accidental poisonings in children.
R.w: The author praises the caps for protecting children yet argues that older adults without children at home should be clearly offered easy-open caps. The view is balanced: keep the caps, but make the alternative known.

n.0: The author says the caps should not be removed from homes with young children, so this goes too far.
n.2: The author notes that federal rules already allow patients to request easy-open caps, so the caps are not an unchangeable requirement.
n.3: The author says the opposite: the caps "have saved countless children."

R.q:
Read the job posting.

Help Wanted: Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA)
Willow Creek Senior Living is hiring full-time and part-time CNAs for day and evening shifts. Requirements: current state CNA certification, CPR certification (or willingness to obtain it within 30 days of hire), and the ability to lift 50 pounds. One year of experience is preferred but not required. Pay starts at $18.50 per hour, with an extra $2.00 per hour for evening shifts and $1.50 per hour for weekend shifts. Full-time staff receive health insurance after 60 days. Apply online or in person, Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Jada holds a current state CNA certification but does not yet have CPR certification or any work experience. She plans to work evening shifts on weekdays. Based on the posting, what would her starting hourly pay be?
R.w: Jada qualifies: CPR can be obtained within 30 days, and experience is preferred, not required. Her base pay is $18.50, plus $2.00 for evening shifts, for $20.50. She works weekdays, so the weekend bonus does not apply.

n.1: Adds the $1.50 weekend addition instead of the $2.00 evening addition.
n.2: Adds both the evening and the weekend additions, but Jada works weekdays.
n.3: Leaves out the $2.00 evening shift addition.

R.q:
Read the original passage and a student's version of it.

Original passage: Although the vaccine is given in two doses spaced a few months apart, many adults who receive the first dose do not return for the second. In one health system, about 60 percent of patients completed the series. When the system began sending text reminders a week before the second dose was due, completion rose to about 80 percent. Patients who received a reminder that included a link to book online were the most likely to return.

Student's version: Many adults skip the second dose of a two-dose vaccine, but reminder texts, especially ones with an online booking link, helped one health system raise completion from about 60 to 80 percent.

Which statement best describes the student's version?
o: It is a summary, because it condenses the main point and key support into fewer words.
It is a paraphrase, because it shifts the original's main point to the booking link.
It is a paraphrase, because it restates the original passage at about the same length.
It is a summary, because it adds the student's own view of why patients skip doses.
R.w: A summary restates the main idea and the most important support in the reader's own words and is shorter than the original. The student's single sentence keeps the problem, the solution and the result in far fewer words, so it is a summary.

n.1: The main point (reminders raised completion) is unchanged; the booking link appears as supporting detail, as in the original.
n.2: A paraphrase stays close to the original's length; the student's version is one sentence compared with four.
n.3: The student adds no personal view; an added opinion would make it a weaker summary, not define one.

R.q:
Passage 1
In 1816, the French physician Rene Laennec needed to listen to a patient's heart but felt uncomfortable pressing his ear to her chest. He rolled a few sheets of paper into a tube, placed one end on her chest, and was surprised by how clearly he could hear. He later built a wooden version and called it a stethoscope.

Passage 2
Hear what you have been missing. The ClearBeat Digital Stethoscope amplifies heart and lung sounds up to 40 times and filters out room noise. Record sounds, share them with colleagues, and replay them in slow motion. Order today and receive a free carrying case.

Which statement best describes how the purposes of the passages differ?
o: Both passages mainly explain the way that a stethoscope makes sounds louder for doctors.
Passage 1 informs readers about the device's origin; Passage 2 urges readers to buy one.
Passage 1 argues for older stethoscopes; Passage 2 informs about recording heart sounds.
Passage 1 entertains with a personal story; Passage 2 explains how digital sound works.
R.w: Passage 1 is a short history of how the stethoscope was invented. Passage 2 is an advertisement with a call to action (Order today) and an offer, so its purpose is to persuade.

n.0: Passage 1 tells how the device was invented, and Passage 2 sells a product; neither mainly explains amplification.
n.2: Passage 1 makes no argument for older devices; it simply recounts the invention.
n.3: Passage 1 uses an anecdote, but to inform about history; and Passage 2 sells a product rather than explaining technology.

R.q:
Read the passage.

When a caller dials 911 in Harlan County, the call first rings at the county's emergency communications center, where a call-taker answers. Before asking about the emergency, the call-taker confirms the caller's location, because a dropped call is useless if no one knows where to go. The call-taker then asks what happened and types the answers into a computer system, which suggests a priority level. A dispatcher, seated at a separate console, reads the entry and radios the nearest available ambulance. While the ambulance is on its way, the call-taker stays on the line and gives the caller first-aid instructions.

Place the steps in the order in which they occur, starting with the first.
o: The call-taker confirms the caller's location
The call-taker asks what happened and enters the answers
The call-taker gives the caller first-aid instructions
The dispatcher radios the nearest available ambulance
The call rings at the emergency communications center
R.w: The call reaches the center and is answered; location is confirmed "before asking about the emergency"; the details are then entered; the dispatcher reads the entry and sends an ambulance; and first-aid instructions come "while the ambulance is on its way."

R.q:
Passage 1
After thirty years with the fire department, Walt retired and found the days long and quiet. On a friend's advice, he began training puppies to become service dogs. Now he spends his mornings teaching them to open doors and pick up dropped keys, and he says he has not felt this useful since his last shift.

Passage 2
When her husband died, Joan stopped going out except to walk her terrier. A neighbor invited her to a community choir, and she went once, then every week. Two years later, Joan organizes the choir's concerts at local hospitals and calls Tuesday rehearsal "the best night of my week."

Which theme do both passages share?
o: A new commitment can restore purpose after a major change.
Music helps people work through grief after a death.
Retirement is harder for people who did physical work.
Pets give steady comfort to people who live on their own.
R.w: Walt finds purpose in training service dogs after retiring, and Joan finds it in the choir after her husband's death. Both show a new commitment filling the gap left by a major life change.

n.1: This fits Passage 2 only; Passage 1 involves no music or death.
n.2: This draws on Passage 1 only and goes beyond it; Passage 1 does not compare kinds of work.
n.3: Dogs appear in both, but that is a minor shared detail; Joan's change comes from the choir, not her terrier.

R.q:
Read the procedure.

In a Fire Emergency, Unit 5
If you see fire or smoke, first remove any patient in immediate danger from the room. Then activate the nearest alarm pull station, unless the alarm is already sounding. Next, close the doors to all patient rooms and stairwells. After closing the doors, report to the nurses' station and give the charge nurse the room number of any patient you moved. Do not use the elevators. If the charge nurse orders an evacuation, move patients horizontally through the fire doors to the next unit before considering the stairs.

Kayla, a nursing assistant, sees smoke coming from room 512. The alarm is silent, and one patient is in the room. Later, the charge nurse orders an evacuation.

Place Kayla's actions in the order the procedure requires, starting with the first.
o: Move patients through the fire doors to the next unit
Close the doors to patient rooms and stairwells
Activate the nearest alarm pull station
Move the patient out of room 512
Give the charge nurse the room number at the nurses' station
R.w: The procedure's order is: remove the patient in danger first; then pull the alarm (required here because the alarm is silent); then close doors; then report the moved patient's room number; and finally, because the charge nurse orders an evacuation, move patients horizontally through the fire doors.

R.q:
Read the description of the organizational chart.

Riverside Medical Center, Nursing Department
Chief Nursing Officer: Dr. Angela Brooks
Reporting directly to Dr. Brooks: Mark Ellis, Director of Inpatient Services; Sofia Ramirez, Director of Outpatient Services; Grace Kim, Director of Nursing Education
Reporting to Mark Ellis: Tom Nguyen, Nurse Manager, Medical-Surgical Unit; Leah Adams, Nurse Manager, Intensive Care Unit
Reporting to Sofia Ramirez: Ben Ortiz, Nurse Manager, Surgery Center; Ruth Hale, Clinic Coordinator
Reporting to Grace Kim: Jamal Price, Clinical Educator
Reporting to Leah Adams: ICU Day Charge Nurse; ICU Night Charge Nurse

According to the chart, to whom does the ICU night charge nurse's direct supervisor report?
o: Leah Adams
Sofia Ramirez
Dr. Angela Brooks
Mark Ellis
R.w: The ICU night charge nurse reports to Leah Adams (step 1). Leah Adams reports to Mark Ellis (step 2), so Mark Ellis is the answer.

n.0: Leah Adams is the charge nurse's direct supervisor; the question asks whom she reports to.
n.1: Sofia Ramirez oversees outpatient services, not the ICU.
n.2: Dr. Brooks is one level higher: Mark Ellis reports to her.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium. The skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to sunlight, but people who live far from the equator make much less of it in winter, when the sun stays low in the sky. A survey in one northern state found that more residents had low vitamin D levels in February than in August. Few foods contain much vitamin D naturally; fatty fish and egg yolks are two exceptions. Many brands of milk and breakfast cereal have vitamin D added during processing.

Based on the passage, which statement is supported?
o: People in northern states should take vitamin D supplements throughout the winter.
Low vitamin D was more common in the surveyed state in late winter than in late summer.
Milk is one of the best natural sources of vitamin D for most people in the country.
A lack of vitamin D causes the bones of adults to soften and weaken over time.
R.w: The passage reports that more residents of the northern state had low levels in February (late winter) than in August (late summer), which matches the explanation about weaker winter sunlight.

n.0: A recommendation the passage never makes.
n.2: Distortion: the passage says vitamin D is added to milk, so milk is not a natural source.
n.3: Outside knowledge: the passage says vitamin D helps absorb calcium but says nothing about bones softening.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a school board report: A review of 30 districts that moved high school start times from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m. found that students slept an average of 40 minutes more on school nights. First-period attendance rose modestly. The board recommends adopting a similar schedule next year.

Passage 2
From a parent's letter: Every morning I watch my son stumble to the bus stop in the dark, too tired to speak. Our teenagers are being asked to learn calculus on five hours of sleep! Other districts have already pushed back the first bell. How many more exhausted years will we accept before we do the same?

Which statement best describes how the two passages relate?
o: The letter favors later start times, while the report stays neutral on the proposed change.
Both favor later start times; the report relies on data and the letter on personal experience.
The report favors later start times, while the letter questions whether they would help.
Both passages question whether early start times have any effect on student attendance.
R.w: The report recommends the later schedule based on a 30-district review; the parent urges the same change based on watching an exhausted son. The tones differ, but the positions agree.

n.0: The report ends by recommending the later schedule, so it is not neutral.
n.2: The letter's emotional tone is not disagreement; the parent asks the district to follow others in pushing back the first bell.
n.3: The report links later starts to better attendance, and the letter never discusses attendance.

R.q:
A reporter for a local paper is revising a story about a zoning meeting. Her editor has asked her to describe both sides in neutral language so that readers can judge the issue for themselves. Her first draft includes this sentence:

The stubborn residents of Oak Street refused to budge on the cell tower, whining that it would ruin their views.

Which revision presents the residents' position without bias?
o: The residents of Oak Street opposed the cell tower, saying it would block their views.
The residents of Oak Street stubbornly opposed the cell tower, saying it would block their views.
The residents of Oak Street complained repeatedly that the cell tower would block their views.
The determined residents of Oak Street bravely stood against the tower to protect their views.
R.w: "Opposed" and "saying" report the residents' position and reason without judging them. The revision removes "stubborn," "refused to budge" and "whining," which all carried negative connotations.

n.1: "Stubbornly" keeps the negative judgment from the original draft.
n.2: "Complained repeatedly" still frames the residents as whiners, so the negative slant remains.
n.3: "Determined" and "bravely" replace a negative slant with a positive one. Bias in favor of a group is still bias.

R.q:
Read the passage.

A local news site asked its readers to vote in an online poll: "Should the town build a new dog park?" Of the 640 readers who voted, 81 percent said yes. The site published the result under the headline "Town Wants Dog Park." The poll was open for two days, and readers could vote more than once by using different devices. The town has about 22,000 residents, and the council has not yet discussed the idea.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Most poll voters favored a dog park, but the poll may not reflect the town.
The news site changed the poll's results to support building a dog park.
Most of the town's 22,000 residents want the town to build a new dog park.
The poll shows that a new dog park would be used by most of the residents.
R.w: The poll shows that 81 percent of its voters said yes. But only 640 people voted in a town of about 22,000, voters chose themselves, and some could vote more than once, so the result may not represent the whole town.

n.1: Unsupported accusation: nothing suggests the site altered results.
n.2: Overgeneralizes from 640 self-selected voters to 22,000 residents, which is the error in the site's headline.
n.3: Goes beyond the evidence: a poll about building a park says nothing about how many people would use it.

R.q:
At a public meeting, several residents asked the hospital's spokesperson why parking fees in the visitor garage had doubled this year. The spokesperson replied, "I understand your concern. But let me tell you about our new rooftop garden, which gives patients a peaceful place to recover. It was funded by donors and has been praised by patients and their families." She then invited the next question, and the parking fees were not discussed again.

Which fallacy does the spokesperson's reply contain?
o: Red herring
Ad hominem
Straw man
Bandwagon
R.w: The question was about parking fees, and the spokesperson shifts attention to the rooftop garden, a topic unrelated to the fees. Distracting from the issue with an irrelevant topic is a red herring.

n.1: The spokesperson does not attack the residents who asked the question.
n.2: A straw man restates the opponent's view in a distorted form; the spokesperson does not restate the residents' concern at all.
n.3: The reply mentions praise for the garden but does not argue that fees are fair because many people agree.

R.q:
Greenway Pharmacy opened a drive-through window in June. The manager tracked the average wait from a customer's arrival to pickup.
Month | Counter wait | Drive-through wait
May | 14 min | not open
June | 11 min | 6 min
July | 10 min | 9 min
August | 10 min | 12 min
The manager noted that drive-through use grew each month as word spread, while one employee continued to staff the window.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage and table?
o: As use of the drive-through grew, its wait became longer than the wait at the counter.
Opening the drive-through cut the counter wait by 4 minutes in each month after May.
Customers prefer the counter to the drive-through because the counter wait is shorter.
Adding a second employee at the window would bring the drive-through wait back to 6 minutes.
R.w: Drive-through use grew every month with one employee, and its wait rose from 6 to 9 to 12 minutes. By August it was longer than the 10-minute counter wait.

n.1: The counter wait fell by 3 minutes in June (14 to 11) and by 4 in July and August, so it did not drop by 4 in each month.
n.2: The passage says drive-through use grew each month, which does not suggest customers prefer the counter.
n.3: This is a prediction the data cannot test; staffing never changed, so the effect of a second employee is unknown.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Emergency departments in many hospitals are crowded not because too many patients arrive, but because admitted patients cannot leave. When the hospital's inpatient beds are full, people who have already been admitted wait in the emergency department, sometimes for a day or more. Their stretchers fill hallways and slow care for new arrivals.

Mercy General tackled the problem by changing its discharge routine. Instead of sending most recovered patients home in the late afternoon, units now aim to complete discharges before 11 a.m., and a team of transport aides helps patients who are waiting for rides. Within a year, the average time admitted patients spent waiting in the emergency department fell from nine hours to four.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Patients who wait in emergency department hallways for a day or more receive slower and less safe care.
Emergency departments are crowded because too many patients come in with minor problems that belong elsewhere.
Admitted patients waiting for beds crowd emergency rooms, and Mercy General cut waits by discharging earlier.
Mercy General hired a team of transport aides to help discharged patients who were waiting for rides home.
R.w: The passage is organized as a problem (admitted patients stuck in the emergency department because beds are full) and a solution (earlier discharges at Mercy General, which cut waits). A summary should state both.

n.0: Distortion: the passage says hallway stretchers slow care for new arrivals; it does not say waiting patients get less safe care.
n.1: Opposite of the passage: the author says crowding is not caused by too many arrivals.
n.3: Too narrow: the transport aides are one part of the solution.

R.q:
On the third day after surgery, the nurse removed Mr. Osei's bandage and checked the incision. The edges had closed, the surrounding skin was only slightly pink, and there was no discharge on the gauze. She recorded that the wound was healing well and told him that the stitches could come out at his follow-up visit.

As used in the passage, the word discharge most nearly means
o: a gap between the edges of a cut.
official release from the hospital.
redness of the skin around a wound.
fluid released from a wound.
R.w: The nurse is examining the gauze over an incision, so the word refers to fluid such as pus or blood coming from the wound. Its absence is a sign of healing.

n.0: The passage says separately that the edges had closed. A gap in the incision is not something that would appear on the gauze.
n.1: Release from the hospital is the most common meaning in a hospital setting, but the word here describes something that would appear on gauze.
n.2: The passage describes the skin's color separately ("only slightly pink"); discharge is something found on the gauze, not a color of the skin.

M.q: A square patio tabletop is 30 inches on each side. A circular hole with a diameter of 10 inches is cut out of the center for an umbrella pole. What is the area of the tabletop that remains? Use 3.14 for pi. Enter the number of square inches.

tr.586: Used the diameter (10 in) as the radius of the hole (3.14 × 100 = 314).
tr.868.6: Subtracted the hole's circumference (31.4 in) instead of its area.
tr.78.5: Gave the area of the hole instead of the area that remains.

M.w: Square = 30 × 30 = 900 in². Hole: r = 5 in, so A = 3.14 × 5² = 78.5 in². Remaining = 900 - 78.5 = 821.5 in².

M.q: A patient's fluid intake on Tuesday was 7/4 of the daily target set by the care team. Which percentage of the target did the patient take in?
M.w: 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75. Multiply by 100 to write it as a percent: 1.75 × 100 = 175%. A value greater than 1 is more than 100%.

n.0: 1.75% puts a percent sign on 1.75 without multiplying by 100.
n.1: 17.5% = 0.175. The decimal point in 1.75 was moved only 1 place right.
n.2: 57.1% is 4 ÷ 7, the reciprocal of 7/4.

M.q: A data set of wait times, in minutes, is 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 38. Which statement about the data set is true?
o: The median of the wait times is 20
The mean exceeds the median
The range of the wait times is 23
The mode of the wait times is 2
M.w: Mean = 140 / 7 = 20. Median = 4th value = 18. 20 > 18, so the mean is greater than the median (the 38 pulls the mean up).

n.0: 20 is the mean; the median is the middle (4th) value, 18.
n.2: 38 - 15 = 23 uses the mode as the minimum; the range is 38 - 12 = 26.
n.3: 15 appears twice; the mode is 15, not the number of times it appears.

M.q: Three coworkers split a $47.83 lunch bill equally. Each person's share is rounded up to the next cent so that the bill is fully covered. How much does each person pay?
M.w: $47.83 ÷ 3 = $15.9433... Rounding up to the next cent gives $15.95. Check: 3 × $15.95 = $47.85, which covers the bill.

n.0: $16.00 rounds up to the next dollar, not the next cent.
n.2: $15.90 rounds down to the nearest ten cents and leaves the bill short.
n.3: $15.94 is ordinary rounding; 3 × $15.94 = $47.82, which is 1 cent short.

M.q: A home health nurse drives 30 miles to a patient's home at an average of 60 miles per hour and returns along the same route at an average of 40 miles per hour. What is her average speed for the whole round trip?
o: 48 miles per hour
40 miles per hour
24 miles per hour
50 miles per hour
M.w: Time out: 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 hour. Time back: 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75 hour. Total: 60 miles in 1.25 hours, so 60 ÷ 1.25 = 48 miles per hour.

n.1: This uses the slower return speed as if it applied to the whole trip.
n.2: This divides the one-way distance of 30 miles by the total time of 1.25 hours.
n.3: This averages the two speeds. Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, and more time is spent at the slower speed.

M.q: A sign is shaped like a parallelogram with a base of 2.5 meters and slanted sides of 1.3 meters. The perpendicular height between the two bases is 1.2 meters. What is the area of one face of the sign?
o: 3 m²
7.6 m²
1.5 m²
M.w: A = base × perpendicular height = 2.5 × 1.2 = 3 m².

n.0: This multiplies the base by the slanted side; the height must be perpendicular to the base.
n.2: 7.6 m is the perimeter, 2 × (2.5 + 1.3), not the area.
n.3: This takes half of base × height, which is the triangle formula.

M.q: The table lists hours of exercise per week (x) and resting heart rate in beats per minute (y) for seven adults: (1, 82), (2, 79), (3, 76), (4, 74), (5, 70), (6, 69), (7, 65). Which statement best describes the relationship shown in a scatterplot of these data?
o: Heart rate tends to fall as weekly exercise hours rise
Exercise hours tend to rise as heart rate rises
There is no correlation, since the drops are uneven
Heart rate falls by exactly 3 beats per extra hour
M.w: As x goes from 1 to 7, y goes from 82 to 65, so y tends to decrease as x increases: a negative correlation.

n.1: Heart rate falls as exercise rises; the two move in opposite directions, not together.
n.2: Uneven drops (3, 3, 2, 4, 1, 4) still form a steady downward trend; no correlation would show no direction at all.
n.3: The drops are 3, 3, 2, 4, 1 and 4 beats, so the decrease is not exactly 3 each hour.

M.q: A health class lists four pairs of variables that could be graphed on scatterplots. Which pair would most likely show a negative correlation?
o: Outdoor temperature and monthly heating cost
Household size and weekly grocery spending
A child's height and arm span
Hours worked and gross weekly pay
M.w: As outdoor temperature rises, less heating is needed, so heating cost tends to fall: one variable increases while the other decreases.

n.1: Larger households tend to spend more on groceries, a positive correlation.
n.2: Taller children tend to have longer arm spans, a positive correlation.
n.3: More hours worked brings more gross pay, a positive correlation.

M.q: A campus store buys a TEAS review book for $28 and marks it up 45% to set the retail price. During a sale, the store takes 20% off the retail price. What is the sale price of the book?

n.1: This is the retail price after the markup; the 20% sale discount still has to be applied.
n.2: This combines the changes as a single 25% markup (45% - 20%). Successive percents multiply: 1.45 × 0.80 = 1.16.
n.3: This takes 20% off the $12.60 markup only instead of off the full $40.60 retail price.

M.q: A dosage calculation gives a volume of 3.96 mL, and the syringe being used is marked in tenths of a milliliter. What is 3.96 rounded to the nearest tenth? Enter the number of milliliters only.

tr.3.1: Rounded the 9 up to 10 but did not carry the 1 into the ones place.

M.w: The tenths digit is 9. The hundredths digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so the 9 rounds up to 10, carrying 1 into the ones place: 3.96 → 4.0 mL (entered as 4).

M.q: A pharmacy has 0.6 g of a powdered drug. Each dose uses 0.003 g. How many doses can be prepared from the powder?
M.w: Move both decimal points 3 places right: 0.6 ÷ 0.003 = 600 ÷ 3 = 200 doses.

n.0: 0.0018 is 0.6 × 0.003; dividing the supply by the dose gives the number of doses.
n.2: 20 moves the decimal point in 0.6 only 2 places while moving 0.003 three places.
n.3: 2,000 moves the decimal point in 0.6 four places while moving 0.003 three places.

M.q: A clinic stocks two sizes of circular wound dressings. The small dressing has a radius of 3 centimeters, and the large dressing has a radius of 6 centimeters. How many more square centimeters does the large dressing cover? Use 3.14 for pi.

n.1: This uses the diameters (6 cm and 12 cm) as the radii.
n.2: This assumes doubling the radius doubles the area; it multiplies the area by 4.
n.3: This is the difference in circumferences (37.68 - 18.84), not in areas.

M.q: A patient's hospital bill is $1,350. The patient first pays a $250 deductible. The insurance plan then pays 80% of the remaining amount, and the patient pays the other 20%. How much does the patient pay in total?
M.w: Remaining after the deductible: 1,350 - 250 = $1,100. Patient's share: 0.20 × 1,100 = $220. Total paid by the patient: 250 + 220 = $470.

n.0: This takes 20% of the full $1,350 and ignores the deductible.
n.1: This is the patient's 20% share of the $1,100 but leaves out the $250 deductible.
n.3: This takes 20% of the full $1,350 ($270) instead of 20% of the $1,100 left after the deductible, then adds $250.

M.q: A stacked bar graph shows clinic visits by age group. The April bar reaches 240 visits in total. Its 'Under 18' segment runs from 0 to 70, its '18 to 64' segment from 70 to 185, and its '65 and older' segment from 185 to 240. To the nearest tenth of a percent, what percent of April visits were by patients aged 18 to 64?
M.w: A middle segment's value is its top minus its bottom: 185 - 70 = 115 visits. 115 / 240 = 0.4792, or 47.9%.

n.1: 185 / 240 = 77.1% reads the top edge of the segment (185) as its value instead of subtracting the 70 below it.
n.2: 55 / 240 = 22.9% is the '65 and older' segment (240 - 185).
n.3: 70 / 240 = 29.2% is the 'Under 18' segment.

M.q: An IV infusion is started at 9:40 a.m. and is programmed to run for 2.6 hours without stopping. At what time will the infusion finish?

n.0: This reads 2.6 hours as 260 minutes (4 h 20 min).
n.1: This reads 2.6 hours as 2 hours 6 minutes; 0.6 h = 0.6 × 60 = 36 min.
n.2: This reads 0.6 hour as 60 minutes, as if an hour had 100 minutes.

M.q: On a medical-surgical unit, the ratio of RNs to LPNs is 5:3. There are 40 nurses on the unit in total. How many of the nurses are LPNs?
M.w: Total parts = 5 + 3 = 8. Each part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 nurses. LPNs = 3 parts × 5 = 15 (and RNs = 25; 15 + 25 = 40).

n.1: This is the number of RNs (5/8 of 40), not LPNs.
n.2: This takes 3/5 of 40, treating the part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole. LPNs are 3 of every 8 nurses.
n.3: This divides 40 into 5 parts. The ratio has 5 + 3 = 8 parts, so each part is 40 ÷ 8 = 5 nurses.

M.q: A cube-shaped gift box has edges 4 inches long. A second cube-shaped box has edges twice as long as the edges of the first box. What is the volume of the second box?
o: 512 in³
256 in³
384 in³
128 in³
M.w: Each edge of the second box is 2 × 4 = 8 in. V = 8³ = 8 × 8 × 8 = 512 in³, which is 8 times the first box's 64 in³.

n.1: This multiplies the volume by 4, which is the scale factor for area, not volume.
n.2: 384 is the surface area of the larger cube in square inches (6 × 8²), not its volume.
n.3: This doubles the first box's volume (2 × 64); doubling every edge multiplies volume by 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

M.q: A medication order is increased to 1.25 times the original dose. Which of the following values are equivalent to 1.25? Select all that apply.
M.w: 1.25 × 100 = 125%. As a fraction, 1.25 = 125/100 = 5/4, and 5/4 = 1 1/4 as a mixed number. All three equal 1.25.

n.0: 12.5% = 0.125. The decimal point was moved only 1 place right.
n.2: 1 1/25 = 1.04. It treats the digits after the decimal point as the denominator.
n.3: 4/5 = 0.8. This is the reciprocal of 5/4.

M.q: A provider orders heparin 7,500 units. The vial is labeled 5,000 units per mL. How many milliliters should be drawn up? Enter the number of milliliters.
M.w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 7,500 ÷ 5,000 × 1 mL = 1.5 mL. As a proportion: 5,000 units/1 mL = 7,500 units/x, so x = 1.5 mL.

M.q: Four specimen containers are labeled with their capacities: container W holds 0.45 L, container X holds 405 mL, container Y holds 4.6 dL, and container Z holds 44 cL. Which container has the greatest capacity?
o: Container Y
Container X
Container Z
Container W
M.w: Convert to milliliters: W = 0.45 × 1,000 = 450 mL; X = 405 mL; Y = 4.6 × 100 = 460 mL; Z = 44 × 10 = 440 mL. Container Y holds the most.

n.1: 405 is the largest number shown, but 405 mL is less than 450 mL and 460 mL.
n.2: 44 cL = 440 mL, which is less than 460 mL.
n.3: 0.45 L = 450 mL, which is less than 4.6 dL = 460 mL.

M.q: A trend line on a scatterplot of weekly study hours (x) and exam score (y) passes through the points (4, 68) and (10, 83). Using the trend line, what exam score is predicted for a student who studies 12 hours per week?
M.w: Slope = (83 - 68) / (10 - 4) = 15 / 6 = 2.5 points per hour. From (10, 83), 2 more hours adds 2 x 2.5 = 5, so the prediction is 88.

n.0: 83 + 2.5 adds the slope once, but 12 hours is 2 hours beyond 10.
n.2: Using 6 / 15 = 0.4 inverts the slope (run over rise), giving 83 + 0.8.
n.3: 83 / 10 x 12 = 99.6 treats the line as passing through the origin (direct variation), but it starts at 58.

M.q: A phlebotomist earns $27.50 per hour plus a flat $165 weekly bonus. Her pay for one week was $1,210, so 27.5h + 165 = 1,210. How many hours, h, did she work that week? Enter the number of hours.

tr.44: Divided 1,210 by 27.50 without first subtracting the $165 bonus.
tr.50: Added the bonus to 1,210 instead of subtracting it.

M.w: Subtract the bonus from both sides: 27.5h = 1,210 - 165 = 1,045. Divide by 27.5: h = 1,045 ÷ 27.5 = 38 hours. Check: 27.5 × 38 = 1,045, and 1,045 + 165 = 1,210.

M.q: A student writes each pair of variables in the form (independent variable, dependent variable). Which pair is written in the correct order?
o: (Hours worked at $18 per hour, weekly paycheck)
(Weekly grocery bill, number of people in the household)
(Distance traveled, hours driven at a steady speed)
(Crop yield, inches of rainfall)
M.w: The paycheck is calculated from the hours worked, so hours worked is independent and the paycheck is dependent; the pair is in the correct order.

n.1: The grocery bill depends on household size, so the order is reversed.
n.2: At a steady speed, distance depends on the hours driven, so the order is reversed.
n.3: Crop yield depends on rainfall, so the order is reversed.

M.q: A clinic orders 3 cases of syringes at $42.75 per case and 5 boxes of alcohol pads at $6.90 per box. A 20% discount applies to the supplies, and then a $12.45 shipping charge is added without a discount. What is the total cost of the order? Enter the amount in dollars, to the nearest cent.

tr.175.2: Added the shipping without applying the discount.
tr.140.16: Applied the 20% discount to the shipping charge as well.

M.q: An advertisement compares a clinic's flu vaccination rate in 2020 and 2025. The rate doubled, so the artist drew the 2025 syringe picture twice as tall and twice as wide as the 2020 picture. Why is the graphic misleading?
o: The 2025 picture is twice as wide, so it understates the increase
The 2025 picture has 2 times the area, which shows the doubling accurately
The 2025 picture has 8 times the area, suggesting an eightfold increase
The 2025 picture has 4 times the area, so the increase looks larger than double
M.w: Scaling both dimensions by 2 multiplies the area by 2 x 2 = 4. Readers judge pictures by area, so a doubling looks like a fourfold increase.

n.0: The extra width makes the increase look larger, not smaller.
n.1: Doubling the height and the width multiplies the area by 4, not 2.
n.2: A factor of 8 (2 x 2 x 2) applies to volume; a flat picture scales its area by 4.

M.q: A survey of 25 households records the number of children in each: 0 children, 4 households; 1 child, 7 households; 2 children, 8 households; 3 children, 4 households; 4 children, 2 households. What is the mean number of children per household? Enter your answer as a decimal.

tr.2: the median or mode, not the mean
tr.5: the mean of the household counts (25 / 5)
tr.8.6: 43 / 5, dividing by the number of categories instead of households

M.q: On an easy 20-point quiz, most students scored from 18 to 20 points, and a few students scored between 5 and 10 points. Which describes the shape of the score distribution and how its mean compares with its median?
o: Skewed right; the mean is greater than the median
Skewed left; the mean is greater than the median
Skewed left; the mean is less than the median
Skewed right; the mean is less than the median
M.w: The few low scores form a long tail on the left, so the distribution is skewed left. Those low scores pull the mean down below the median.

n.0: This names the skew by where the scores pile up (the right); skew is named for the tail, which is on the left.
n.1: The shape is right, but the low tail pulls the mean below the median, not above it.
n.3: The tail is on the left, so the distribution is skewed left, not right.

M.q: The annual salaries, in thousands of dollars, of the seven employees at a small clinic are 42, 45, 45, 48, 51, 54, and 160. How much greater is the mean salary than the median salary, in thousands of dollars? Round to the nearest tenth.

tr.18.6: mean minus the mode (45) instead of the median

M.w: Sum = 445, so mean = 445 / 7 = 63.57. Median = 4th value = 48. Difference = 63.57 - 48 = 15.57, about 15.6 thousand dollars.

M.q: At 6:00 p.m. the outdoor temperature is 38°F, and it falls 4°F each hour. The expression 38 - 4h gives the temperature h hours after 6:00 p.m. For which values of h will the temperature be below 10°F?
M.w: Write 38 - 4h < 10. Subtract 38: -4h < -28. Divide by -4 and reverse the sign: h > 7. Check h = 8: 38 - 32 = 6°F, which is below 10°F.

n.1: This adds 10 to 38 instead of subtracting it, giving 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
n.2: This adds 10 to 38 instead of subtracting it and also keeps the sign when dividing by -4.
n.3: This divides by -4 without reversing the inequality sign.

M.q: A pharmacy technician writes a phrase from a dosing worksheet as an algebraic expression. Which expression represents 'six less than the quotient of a number n and 4'?
M.w: 'The quotient of a number n and 4' is n/4. 'Six less than' that quotient subtracts 6 from it, so the expression is n/4 - 6.

n.0: 'Six less than' a quantity subtracts 6 from that quantity, so the quotient comes first: n/4 - 6, not 6 - n/4.
n.2: 'The quotient of n and 4' means n divided by 4. Writing 4/n reverses the division.
n.3: This subtracts 6 before dividing. The quotient n/4 is formed first, and then 6 is taken away.

M.q: Four lab measurements are recorded as 1.105, 1 1/8, 1.09 and 112%. Place the measurements in order from greatest to least, starting with the greatest.
A container of protein powder holds 2 pounds of powder. Each scoop holds 30 grams. Use 1 ounce = 28 grams. How many full scoops of powder does the container hold?
M.w: 2 lb × 16 = 32 oz. 32 × 28 = 896 g. 896 ÷ 30 = 29.87, so the container holds 29 full scoops.

n.0: This multiplies 2 lb by 2.2 as if converting to kilograms (4.4 kg); pounds to kilograms means dividing.
n.1: This uses 10 ounces per pound (20 oz = 560 g); 1 lb = 16 oz.
n.3: 896 ÷ 30 = 29.9, and the 30th scoop would not be full, so round down.

M.q: Solve for x: x/3 + x/4 = 14.
M.w: Multiply every term by the LCD, 12: 4x + 3x = 168. Combine: 7x = 168. Divide by 7: x = 24. Check: 24/3 + 24/4 = 8 + 6 = 14.

n.1: This adds the numerators and the denominators, treating the sum as 2x/7.
n.2: This multiplies the left side by 12 but not the right side, giving 7x = 14. Every term must be multiplied by 12.
n.3: This adds the denominators, treating x/3 + x/4 as x/7. With a common denominator, 4x/12 + 3x/12 = 7x/12.

M.q: A lab technician multiplies two measurements and gets a product of 0.0024. Which multiplication gives a product of exactly 0.0024?
M.w: 4 × 6 = 24. In 0.04 × 0.06 the factors have 2 + 2 = 4 decimal places, so the product is 0.0024.

n.1: 0.004 × 0.06 has 5 decimal places in total, so the product is 0.00024.
n.2: 0.4 × 0.06 has 3 decimal places in total, so the product is 0.024.
n.3: 0.4 × 0.6 has 2 decimal places in total, so the product is 0.24.

M.q: The table lists hours studied (x) and exam score (y) for seven students: (2, 61), (3, 66), (4, 70), (5, 52), (6, 79), (7, 83), (8, 88). When the data are graphed on a scatterplot, which point does not fit the overall trend?
M.w: Scores rise about 4 to 5 points per extra hour, so a student who studied 5 hours would be expected to score about 74. A score of 52 sits far below the pattern.

n.0: (8, 88) is the highest point, but it continues the upward trend.
n.1: (4, 70) is about 4 points above (3, 66), in line with the trend.
n.3: (2, 61) has the lowest x-value, and its score fits the rising pattern from the left.

M.q: A patient has a fluid allowance of 1,200 mL for the day. She uses 1/4 of the allowance at breakfast, and then 2/3 of the remaining amount over lunch and dinner. How many milliliters are left for the evening?
o: 900 mL
300 mL
600 mL
100 mL
M.w: Breakfast: 1/4 × 1,200 = 300 mL, leaving 900 mL. Lunch and dinner: 2/3 × 900 = 600 mL, leaving 900 - 600 = 300 mL for the evening.

n.0: This is the amount left after breakfast, an intermediate step; lunch and dinner still have to be subtracted.
n.2: This is the amount used at lunch and dinner, not the amount left.
n.3: This takes 2/3 of the full 1,200 mL instead of 2/3 of the 900 mL remaining after breakfast.

M.q: On Monday a checking account was at -45 dollars, and on Tuesday it was at 30 dollars. Which expression gives the distance between -45 and 30 on a number line?
M.w: Distance between a and b is |b - a|: |30 - (-45)| = |30 + 45| = 75.

n.0: |30| - |-45| = 30 - 45 = -15; a difference of absolute values is not the distance.
n.2: 30 - 45 = -15 drops the negative sign of -45 and gives a negative distance.
n.3: |30 + (-45)| = 15 adds the numbers instead of subtracting them.

M.q: An architect builds a model of a new hospital wing at a scale of 1:200. The model is 45 centimeters tall. How tall will the actual building be, in meters? (1 meter = 100 centimeters)
o: 0.225 meters
90 meters
9 meters
900 meters
M.w: Each model centimeter represents 200 actual centimeters: 45 × 200 = 9,000 cm. Convert: 9,000 ÷ 100 = 90 meters.

n.0: This divides the model height by 200 instead of multiplying; the real building is larger than the model.
n.2: This divides 9,000 cm by 1,000 instead of 100; there are 100 cm in a meter.
n.3: This divides 9,000 cm by 10 instead of 100; there are 100 cm in a meter.

S.q: A chemistry teacher writes the freezing point of pure water at sea level on three different temperature scales. Which set shows the same temperature on all three scales?
S.w: Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F = 273 K (K = °C + 273).

n.0: 373 K is the boiling point of water (100 °C), not the freezing point.
n.1: 0 K is absolute zero, about -273 °C, far below the freezing point of water.
n.2: 0 °F is about -18 °C; water freezes at 32 °F.

S.q: Moving from left to right across period 3, from sodium to chlorine, how does atomic radius change, and what explains the change?
o: It increases, because each element adds more electrons
It increases, because a new electron shell is added each time
